concepts.title: Totipotency and the History of Plant Tissue Culture

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Totipotency and the History of Plant Tissue Culture' refers to.
questions.a: Every living plant cell keeps the totipotent power to regenerate a whole plant, the intuition Haberlandt advanced in 1902 that earned him the fatherhood of the field; kinetin arrived in 1955, the Skoog-Miller 1957 ratio rule tied organ fate to hormone balance, Murashige and Skoog's 1962 salt-rich medium became the standard, and Guha and Maheshwari's 1964 anther-culture haploids opened the door to somatic hybrids, Pomato of 1978 and the somaclonal variation named in 1981.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Totipotency and the History of Plant Tissue Culture'.
questions.a: One vegetative cell can rebuild the entire plant - the promise that turned tissue culture into both a science and an industry.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Totipotency and the History of Plant Tissue Culture' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Explant Preparation and Culture Steps' refers to.
questions.a: Culturing starts with an explant - meristem, leaf, cotyledon, hypocotyl or embryo - surface-sterilised in sodium hypochlorite, rinsed and inoculated onto sterile medium; the tissue then dedifferentiates into callus, redifferentiates organ primordia through organogenesis or follows somatic embryogenesis, with regenerated shoots rooted and plantlets hardened toward the field, immature embryos responding best among explant choices.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Explant Preparation and Culture Steps'.
questions.a: Sterilise, inoculate, dedifferentiate, redifferentiate, root and harden - the pipeline from explant to field-ready plantlet.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Explant Preparation and Culture Steps' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Micropropagation and Synthetic Seeds' refers to.
questions.a: Micropropagation clones elite, rare or non-fertile plants season-free in flasks - India alone regenerates over 400 million banana plantlets a year - while synthetic seeds encapsulate somatic embryos in calcium alginate coats loaded with nutrients and regulators, storing and shipping clonal stock of carrot, grape or sandalwood without any seed at all.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Micropropagation and Synthetic Seeds'.
questions.a: Multiply one elite genotype into millions, then pack the embryos in alginate beads that behave like true seeds.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Micropropagation and Synthetic Seeds' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Meristem Culture for Virus-Free Plants' refers to.
questions.a: Viruses scatter unevenly through plant bodies and leave the apical and axillary meristems clean, so excising a meristem tip shorter than one millimetre and culturing it regenerates sugarcane, banana or potato stock entirely free of virus - rescuing yields in clonally propagated crops where every infected cutting infects its whole lineage.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Meristem Culture for Virus-Free Plants'.
questions.a: Take the tiniest meristem - under a millimetre - where no virus has reached, and grow a clean clone from it.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Meristem Culture for Virus-Free Plants' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Somaclonal Variation and Secondary Metabolites' refers to.
questions.a: Culture both creates and harvests plant chemistry: somaclonal variations - the term Larkin and Scowcroft coined in 1981 - pass somatic mutations into regenerated plants, a bane for clonal fidelity but a boon yielding disease-resistant sugarcane, banana and tomato cultivars; meanwhile cell suspensions and hairy roots overproduce secondary metabolites from artemisinin and azadirachtin to taxol, shikonin and vincristine, independent of season and without stripping wild populations.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Somaclonal Variation and Secondary Metabolites'.
questions.a: Culture-induced variants can be screened as new cultivars, and cultured cells can out-produce the whole plant in valuable metabolites.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Somaclonal Variation and Secondary Metabolites' taught, and from which source text?
